title: 10 - Yes, 10! - Dumb Criminals
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck open with tour dates (Medford MA, Washington DC, NYC Town Hall, and August and September shows) and then present a "top ten" countdown of dumb criminal stories, with a few digressions into movies, TV and books. Cases include Maganga's failed carjacking in Omaha, Derreck Moseley's gun store robbery in Oregon, Joey Miller and Matthew McNelly's marker-face break-in attempt in Iowa, the apocryphal Klaus Schmidt bank story, James Blankenship's daytime burglary of his mother's house in Ohio, Darren Kempton's double break-in in England, Ruben Zarati's muffler shop robbery set-up in Chicago, Albert Bailey's Fairfield, Connecticut bank robbery, and James Washington's deathbed confession in Nashville. The episode closes with a listener email about a childhood dog poop fight.

segments.title: Tour dates announcement
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck announce upcoming live shows in Medford MA, Washington DC, New York City Town Hall, and later August and September dates in Chicago, Minneapolis, Indianapolis, Durham, and Atlanta, with ticket info.

segments.title: Opening banter and premise
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the episode as a top ten list of dumb criminals and explain Josh's skepticism about such lists, deciding to take the stories at face value.

segments.title: Maganga stick shift carjacking
segments.summary: A seventeen-year-old named Maganga in Omaha, Nebraska, attempted a carjacking in 2014 at about 7 a.m., but could not drive the manual transmission car and was arrested on foot after about seven minutes.

segments.title: Derreck Moseley gun store robbery
segments.summary: Derreck Moseley robbed Discount Gun Sales in Washington County, Oregon, with a baseball bat and knife, smashed a display case, and was stopped when the manager drew a gun. He received five years probation and paid $350 for the case.

segments.title: Joey Miller and Matthew McNelly marker disguise
segments.summary: In October 2009 in Carroll, Iowa, Joey Miller and Matthew McNelly tried to break into a man's home wearing hoodies and scribbled permanent marker on their faces. They were stopped by police who matched them to a witness description, and charges were later dismissed because there was no evidence they entered the apartment.

segments.title: Klaus Schmidt apocryphal bank robbery
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Klaus Schmidt story of a deaf Berlin bank robber in August 1995 who was supposedly set off an alarm the tellers thought he could not hear. They note they could find no record of Klaus Schmidt and that the story is likely an urban legend.

segments.title: James Blankenship daytime burglary
segments.summary: James Blankenship tried to rob his own mother's house in broad daylight in Willoughby, Ohio, in June 2013, and was arrested after hiding in a crawl space. He believed burglary only happens at night; the hosts explain the old common law definition required nighttime, and the modern definition is about illegal entry with intent to commit a crime, especially theft.

segments.title: Darren Kempton second break-in
segments.summary: Darren Kempton in Abington, England, in 2013 broke into a house earlier that day and then attempted a second break-in at a house that police were already inside investigating. He left a blood trail linking him to the first crime.

segments.title: Hunter S. Thompson and tangents
segments.summary: Following the Darren Kempton story, the hosts digress into Hunter S. Thompson's writing and his stumbling into a police convention, and discuss their feelings about Jim Morrison's poetry and Bukowski.

segments.title: Ruben Zarati muffler shop robbery
segments.summary: In 2008 in Chicago, eighteen-year-old Ruben Zarati was told by muffler shop manager Jose Cedeno to return later with his number so he could rob the store. Cedeno had called police, and when Zarati entered officers opened fire, shooting him in the back. Zarati survived with surgery and later sued the city.

segments.title: Albert Bailey Fairfield bank robbery
segments.summary: In 2010 in Fairfield, Connecticut, Albert Bailey phoned a bank ahead to announce a robbery, then sent his sixteen-year-old cousin inside with a briefcase. Police arrived, Bailey surrendered, and the hosts note his claim of being forced by a bomb-wearing kidnapper, similar to the 2003 Brian Wells collar bomb case.

segments.title: Movie and TV recommendations tangent
segments.summary: The hosts discuss films by Yorgos Lanthimos including The Lobster and The Killing of a Sacred Deer, Colin Farrell, Black Swan, and Swan Lake at the Kennedy Center.

segments.title: TV recommendations: Ripley and Fallout
segments.summary: Chuck recommends the Netflix series Ripley, based on Patricia Highsmith's Tom Ripley novels, praising its black-and-white cinematography by Robert Elswit and its cast. He also mentions the Fallout TV show with Walton Goggins.

segments.title: James Washington Nashville deathbed confession
segments.summary: In Nashville around 2009, James Washington, serving fifteen years for attempted murder, confessed to a prison guard during a heart attack that he had murdered Joyce Goodner in 1995. He recovered and tried to recant, but was given a life sentence based on his confession.

segments.title: Listener mail: white dog poop fight
segments.summary: Listener Alan White shares a childhood memory from fifth grade in 1955 of a fight with neighbor Jerry using white dog poop.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the listener mail segment and sign off with the iHeartRadio credit and podcast listing info.
